Let’s talk about something that comes up a lot in open relationships—jealousy, and all those tricky emotional challenges that can tag along.
You know, a lot of people worry that jealousy will be an impossible hurdle, or they think folks in non-monogamous relationships just don’t feel it. But that’s not the case. Jealousy is totally normal—it’s just part of being human. The thing is, learning how to handle it is a big part of what makes open relationships work.
Usually, jealousy pops up because of fear. Maybe it’s the fear of losing someone you love, being replaced, or not feeling like you’re enough. Sometimes, it’s old insecurities, past hurts, or just the messages we’ve picked up that say “real love” means being exclusive. Instead of treating jealousy like a sign you’re failing, ethical non-monogamy asks you to see it as a chance to learn about yourself and grow.
Here’s the first step: just admit to yourself when you’re feeling jealous—without beating yourself up. Trying to ignore or bury those feelings usually just makes them stronger. So, get curious. What’s really underneath that jealousy? Maybe you’re craving more attention, needing reassurance, or just looking for a little more security. If you can figure out what you truly need, you’re already halfway there.
There are a few strategies that can really help when jealousy or other tough emotions show up.
One is self-soothing. That might mean taking a mindful pause, writing in a journal, or reaching out to a friend who “gets it.”
Another is reframing. Instead of seeing your partner’s other relationships as threats, what if you saw them as something that brings more joy and richness into their life—and maybe even into yours? Love isn’t a pie with only so many slices to go around.
Then there’s requesting reassurance. If you’re feeling vulnerable, it’s okay to ask for what you need—maybe some extra time together, or just a few words to remind you that you matter.
And don’t forget about setting boundaries. Be clear about what feels safe for you, and talk openly about those needs.
Picture this: you notice a twinge of jealousy when your partner goes out with someone else. Instead of lashing out or shutting down, you pause and check in with yourself. Maybe you ask for a little reassurance, or suggest spending some quality time together soon. Over time, these small steps can actually turn jealousy into something that deepens your connection and helps you understand yourself better.
It’s also worth remembering: jealousy doesn’t always mean something’s wrong. Sometimes, it’s just a gentle nudge that you’re wanting more closeness, or maybe it’s time to check in on your own self-care. Other times, it’s a sign that a boundary or agreement needs updating.
Alongside jealousy, you might bump into feelings like envy, insecurity, or that classic fear of missing out. It’s all normal. When you talk about these feelings openly, it can actually make your relationship stronger and more resilient. And if things get tough, reaching out to friends, community, or even a counselor can make a world of difference.
So, here’s the key takeaway: the goal isn’t to wipe out all difficult emotions. It’s about learning how to move through them—with kindness, for yourself and for your partners. By facing jealousy and other challenges head-on, you can build relationships that are both flexible and deeply rooted in real care.
